title: How an instruction becomes bits
objective: By the end of this lesson you can encode a RISC-V instruction by hand, decode one back into its fields, and explain why the register count and the field widths are the same fact.

blocks.text: An instruction is a 32-bit number. Everything the processor needs — which operation, which registers, which constant — is packed into those bits at fixed positions. Encoding one by hand takes a few minutes and removes most of the mystery from everything that follows.
The fields of a register-register instruction

blocks.caption: The R-type layout, bit positions from the specification
lines: 7 bits    5 bits   5 bits  3 bits  5 bits    7 bits
opcode  which family of instruction this is
funct3  which operation within the family
funct7  further refinement — this is what separates add from sub

blocks.title: The register count is a consequence of the field width
blocks.text: A register field is 5 bits, and 5 bits can name 32 things — which is why the architecture has 32 registers. It is not that someone chose 32 and then sized the field; the instruction had to fit in 32 bits, three register fields had to fit in it alongside the operation, and 5 bits each was what remained. The number of registers you can use is an arithmetic consequence of the encoding.

blocks.caption: add x5, x6, x7 — computed field by field
lines: funct7   rs2   rs1  f3   rd    opcode

blocks.caption: The same instruction with one field changed
lines: /* Addition and subtraction share an opcode and a funct3. They are
distinguished by a single bit in funct7, because the hardware that
performs them is the same hardware with one control input flipped. */

blocks.caption: The I-type layout, and addi x5, x6, 42
lines: /* rs2 and funct7 are gone; their 12 bits became the constant. */
decoded back: opcode=0010011  rd=x5  funct3=000  rs1=x6  imm=42

blocks.title: Twelve bits is why large constants need several instructions
blocks.text: An immediate field of 12 bits holds values from -2048 to 2047. Anything larger cannot be encoded in one instruction, which is exactly what the previous lesson measured: a 64-bit constant on aarch64 took three instructions to assemble. The limit you saw in generated code is this field width, and now you can point at where it comes from.
Why the fields sit where they do

items: opcode is at the bottom, so the decoder can read it first and know which layout the rest follows
rd is in the same position in every format, so the register file can be addressed before decoding finishes
rs1 and rs2 are likewise fixed, for the same reason
The immediate is split across odd positions in some formats specifically to keep those register fields aligned

blocks.text: That last point looks like a mistake when you first see the branch and store formats, whose immediates are scattered across non-contiguous bits. It is deliberate: keeping rs1, rs2 and rd in fixed places lets the hardware start fetching register values while it is still working out what the instruction means. Reassembling a scattered immediate is free in hardware — it is only wiring — while a shifted register field would cost a multiplexer on the critical path.

blocks.title: Encode and decode by hand
steps: Encode add x10, x11, x12 by hand and write the hexadecimal result
Encode sub x10, x11, x12 and confirm it differs from add by exactly bit 30
Encode addi x10, x11, 100 and decode your own answer back into fields
Try to encode addi x10, x11, 5000 and explain why it does not fit
Write a small decoder in any language that takes a 32-bit word and prints the fields
Feed it 0x007302b3 and 0x02a30293 and confirm you recover the original instructions
If you have a RISC-V toolchain, assemble the same instructions and compare with your hand encoding
blocks.expected: Two hand encodings that match a calculator, a one-bit difference between add and sub that you predicted, and a decoder of your own that recovers the fields. Once you can do this, the datapath in the next module reads as a picture of what your decoder just did in software.

cheatsheet: An instruction is a 32-bit number with fields at fixed bit positions
I-type: immediate[31:20] rs1[19:15] funct3[14:12] rd[11:7] opcode[6:0]
A 5-bit register field names 32 registers — that is why there are 32
add x5,x6,x7 is 0x007302b3; sub is 0x407302b3; they differ by bit 30 alone
A 12-bit immediate holds -2048 to 2047 — larger constants need several instructions
opcode sits at the bottom so the decoder reads it first
Register fields stay in fixed positions so the register file can be read during decoding

checkpoint.prompt: Why does this architecture have exactly 32 registers?

choices.A: A register field is 5 bits, and 5 bits name 32 things
choices.B: 32 was found to be optimal by measurement on real code

checkpoint.explanation: The instruction had to fit in 32 bits with three register fields plus the operation. Five bits each was what remained, and 2 to the fifth is 32. The count follows from the encoding.

checkpoint.prompt: add and sub have the same opcode and the same funct3. How does the hardware tell them apart?

choices.A: They are the same instruction under two names

checkpoint.explanation: The two encodings differ by bit 30 alone. 0x007302b3 against 0x407302b3. One bit, because the hardware that adds and the hardware that subtracts are the same unit with one control input flipped.

checkpoint.prompt: Why can an I-type instruction not hold a constant of 5000?

choices.D: Constants must be powers of two

checkpoint.explanation: Covers -2048 to 2047. This is the field width you can now point at, and it is the same limit that made a 64-bit constant take three instructions in the previous lesson's measured example.

checkpoint.prompt: Why are register fields kept at the same bit positions in every instruction format?

choices.A: It is an accident of history
choices.B: To simplify the assembler, which needs only one pass
choices.C: So register reads can start before decode finishes

checkpoint.explanation: It is why some formats scatter their immediate across non-contiguous bits: reassembling those in hardware is just wiring, while a shifted register field would add a multiplexer to the critical path.
